name: NorthOS
tagline: A Canadian SaaS pitched as an operating system for running a business: dashboards, records and day-to-day work in one place.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Anything that calls itself an OS is really a bundle: some tables, some views, some workflow, one login. A coding agent can absolutely produce your personal version of that bundle, because a single-user app does not need permissions, audit trails, or an admin panel for a team of twelve. Where it stops being cute is the plumbing around the edges: accounting and payroll connectors, imports from whatever you are running today, mobile, and the fact that a business tool other people depend on has to actually stay up. Our read on this specific product is thin, so treat the verdict as shape-level rather than feature-level. If you are one person tracking your own operation, build it. If it runs a company with staff, do not make yourself the on-call engineer.
coreLoopDIY: A local, single-user workspace with custom record types, list and board views, linked records, and a home dashboard of saved queries.
requirements: Node 20 and a local Postgres or SQLite file
A VPS or home box if you want it reachable outside your laptop
Your own backup routine, this becomes the only copy of your operational data
Manual CSV export from whatever tool you are leaving
whatYouLose: Integrations with accounting, payroll, banking, and whatever else the vendor already wired up
Multi-user reality: roles, permissions, invites, someone else's audit log
Mobile access that is not just your site rendered badly on a phone
Support you can email when the thing holding your operations breaks
Ongoing feature work, your build is frozen the day you stop caring
moatNotes: The lock-in is not the feature list, it is that once your records, workflows and habits live inside it, moving costs a quarter.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the software is the cheap part. What a business actually buys is someone else being responsible for uptime, backups, the connector to their accountant's system, and the answer to "why can Dave see this". A one-person clone skips all of that by definition, which is fine when the one person is you and terrible when it is a team of fifteen with an invoicing deadline.
notes: The tables and views are a weekend; the integrations and the being-responsible-for-it are not.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user business workspace app. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript
- SQLite via Drizzle ORM, file at ./data/app.db
- Tailwind CSS, no component library
- Zod for validation
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost, nothing else required

Core model:
- Collections: user-defined record types with a name, icon, and an ordered field schema
- Field types: text, longtext, number, currency, date, select (with options), checkbox, url, and relation (points at another collection)
- Records: rows in a collection, stored as JSON validated against the collection schema at write time
- Views: saved per collection, either table or board (board groups by a select field), with filters, sort, and visible-column config
- Dashboard: home page of user-chosen widgets, each widget is a saved view rendered as a count, a sum of one numeric field, or a compact list

UI requirements:
- Left sidebar lists collections and saved views
- Table view supports inline editing, keyboard up/down/enter navigation, and column resize
- Record detail as a right-side drawer showing fields plus related records
- Global search across all text fields, hotkey cmd+k
- Schema editor UI for adding, renaming, reordering, and deleting fields, with a confirm step on delete

Data handling:
- CSV import that previews rows and lets me map columns to fields before committing
- CSV and full JSON export per collection
- `npm run backup` script that copies the SQLite file to ./backups with a timestamp

Explicitly out of scope, do not build:
- Auth, users, roles, invites, sharing
- Any third-party integration, OAuth, webhooks, or email sending
- Real-time collaboration or websockets
- Mobile app, a responsive layout is enough

Seed the database with two example collections (Clients, Jobs) linked by a relation field, about twenty fake rows total. Put any config in .env with a committed .env.example. Write a README that says plainly: single user, local only, back up the db file yourself.
